Sample text:
---
**The Jar System**

After my father died, I inherited the workshop, which is to say I inherited eleven hundred jars.

They lined the walls on shelves he had built himself, slightly crooked, each one leaning a degree or two toward the window as if the whole room were trying to look outside. Mason jars, pickle jars, baby food jars with the labels soaked off. Every one was full of small metal things: screws, washers, nuts, brads, cotter pins, hinges no bigger than a fingernail, and keys that opened nothing anyone could name.

My sister wanted to sell the building and hire someone to haul it all away. "It's scrap," she said on the phone. "Sixty years of scrap."

"I'll spend a weekend," I said. "Just to see."

I drove out on a Friday. The workshop smelled the way it always had, of machine oil, cedar shavings, and the burnt-coffee ghost of a percolator he never stopped using. I stood in the doorway a long time before I touched anything. When I did, I picked up a jar at random, one near the middle of the east wall, and held it to the light.

Screws. But not just screws. Brass ones, all about an inch long, all with slightly rounded heads. In the next jar, brass screws again, but shorter. In the next, brass with slotted heads gone soft, as if they'd been turned many times.

I had assumed there was no system. My father was a man who alphabetized nothing, who kept his tax returns in a boot. But the longer I looked, the more the shelves seemed to be arguing a point, quietly, in a language I almost knew.

I spent Friday night learning the obvious rules. Size, then material, then head type. Simple enough. But there were exceptions that bothered me. A single steel screw sat in a jar of brass ones. A jar of identical black washers had one copper washer at the bottom, like a coin in a fountain. I found a whole jar of mismatched bolts labeled, on a strip of masking tape, *Tuesday.*

I slept on the cot in the back, under the wool blanket that smelled like him, and dreamed of nothing.

On Saturday I started opening jars and dumping them onto the bench, because that is what you do when you want to understand something: you take it apart. The steel screw in the brass jar had a scratch on its shaft. The copper washer had a tiny notch filed into its edge. The bolts labeled *Tuesday* were all different, but each had a smear of the same green paint on the threads.

That paint I recognized. He had painted our porch that green the summer I was nine. I'd held the ladder. He'd let me use the brush on the bottom step, the one nobody would see, and I'd gotten more on my shoes than on the wood. He'd laughed and said, "That's a good step. That's the most honest step in the house."

I sat down on the stool.

So it wasn't a system of size or material. Or it was, but only at the surface, the way the alphabet is a system for a novel. Underneath, each jar was a kind of drawer of days. The screws from the porch. The washers from the winter the furnace failed, black with soot, the copper one from the pipe he'd soldered by flashlight while I held the light and my mother slept upstairs, unaware how close we'd come to something worse than cold. The brass screws with soft heads came from the cabinet hinges in my grandmother's kitchen, which he'd removed when she died and replaced with new ones, keeping the old.

He hadn't been hoarding. He had been filing.

By noon I'd stopped trying to sort anything. I walked the shelves slowly, opening lids and smelling the metal, that cold, coin-on-the-tongue smell, and finding a memory in almost every one. Not my memories, exactly. A jar of tiny screws from eyeglasses, and I thought of his reading glasses, always halfway down his nose. A jar of buttons and rivets from a work jacket. A jar of piano pins, though we never owned a piano, and I would never learn why.

Some I couldn't decode at all. Those were the ones that got me. Whole shelves in the back corner were jars that meant something to a man who no longer existed to say what. That's what dying is, I thought, at the level of objects. The meaning goes out of the world and the things stay behind, faithful and mute.

At three o'clock I called my sister.

"I don't think we can just throw it away," I said.

"It's *screws*," she said, but gently. She'd been crying, I could tell. She'd been crying for a week, in the way she does, efficiently, between tasks.

"Come out here," I said. "Come out and pick a jar. Any jar. Just tell me what you see."

She was quiet. Then: "Is the percolator still there?"

"Yes."

"Make coffee. I'll be there in two hours."

She arrived at five, in her work clothes, with her car keys still in her fist as if she might leave. I handed her a jar without explanation. It was small, a baby food jar, and inside were maybe thirty tiny silver screws.

She turned it in the light. "These are from the toy," she said slowly. "The robot. The one with the eyes that lit up."

"You remember it?"

"I broke it. I took it apart to see how the eyes worked, and I couldn't put it back, and I hid it under my bed for a month." She laughed, wet and startled. "He found it. He never said a word about it. He just fixed it and left it on my pillow."

"And kept the screws he didn't need."

"He kept the ones that were left over," she said. "Dad always had left-over screws. He said that was how you knew you'd done it right, that a job with no extras was a job with something missing."

We stood in the amber light, holding the jar between us like a small lantern.

We didn't sell the building that year. Eventually we did, to a young woman who repairs bicycles and who promised, without being asked, to keep the shelves. But that night we stayed until dark, opening jars, saying *this one*, saying *remember*, and the workshop, leaning toward its window, seemed to lean a little further, listening.

Before I left I took one jar for myself. It was the *Tuesday* jar, the mismatched bolts with their green-smeared threads. I don't know what Tuesday it was. I've decided that's all right.

Some things you keep so you'll know. Some you keep so you'll have kept them.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A carefully shaped grief story uses a workshop full of jars to turn family memory into something tactile and shared.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, observant, and quietly elegiac. It lets grief gather through small particulars—the crooked shelves, the percolator, a jar of toy screws—rather than announcing it at the outset. The story’s pathos comes from discovering that the father’s apparent clutter was a private archive, and from the siblings recovering different memories through it. The closing thought offers the reader a gentle distinction between keeping something to understand it and keeping it simply because it was once held.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds inheritance, grief, and the uncertain meanings objects carry after their owners are gone. Jars and leftover screws become records of ordinary acts of care: fixing a toy, saving old hinges, working through a cold night. The story treats attention and remembrance as forms of love, while leaving some objects—and some knowledge—unresolved.

## Evidence line
> The meaning goes out of the world and the things stay behind, faithful and mute.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent motif of ordinary objects carrying grief and care is unusually well sustained, though the story’s polished, familiar elegiac shape makes its voice less distinctive than its central image.
